💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch.
  • Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing complications with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.
  • We know that Season 2 is introducing a big newly introduced map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing complications with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a big newly introduced map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

According to recent reports, the real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the fresh season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

According to recent reports, BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

#132371. Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1610 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug.
  • The findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney.
  • Psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A major international analysis has found that people who use cannabis experience their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than those who do not use the drug. Even more concerning, the difference becomes substantially larger with age, reaching more than six years among people who develop psychosis in their 30s or later.

The findings, published in the journal Biological Psychiatry, come from researchers at UNSW Sydney. They suggest that the potential psychiatric consequences of cannabis use may extend well beyond adolescence and could become more pronounced with prolonged exposure.

Psychosis is a condition in which a person experiences a disruption in their perception of reality. Symptoms can include hallucinations, false beliefs known as delusions, and disturbances in thinking or behavior. It can occur in schizophrenia and several other mental health disorders. Although psychosis most commonly begins during the late teenage years or early adulthood, it can develop at other stages of life. According to Psychosis Australia, up to 3% of adults will experience a diagnosed disorder involving psychosis during their lifetime.

Cannabis Linked to Earlier Psychosis Across Adulthood.

To investigate the relationship between cannabis use and the timing of psychosis, researchers at UNSW Medicine analyzed 149 studies involving more than 71,000 participants. Most of the research had been conducted since 2011 in Europe, North America, and Australia, with the majority of studies focusing on people diagnosed with schizophrenia.

The researchers discovered that the difference in the age at which psychosis first appeared varied considerably across age groups.

Recent findings suggest that in studies where the average age of psychosis onset was between 20 and 24, cannabis people experienced their first episode approximately 1.6 years earlier than non-users. That difference widened to 4.43 years in studies involving people whose psychosis emerged in their mid-to-late 20s (25-29).

The largest difference appeared in studies where psychosis developed at age 30 or later. In this group, cannabis consumers experienced the condition an average of 6.3 years earlier than non-users.

These results suggest that the association between cannabis and earlier psychosis may become stronger as people grow older, potentially reflecting the effects of longer periods of cannabis exposure.

Why Cannabis Risks May Increase With Age.

Chief investigator Matthew Large, a psychiatrist and Conjoint Professor at UNSW's School of Clinical Medicine, stated the findings raise notable questions about the long-term psychiatric effects of cannabis.

It has been revealed that "We've tended to focus on the dangers of using cannabis in adolescence, when the brain is still developing, but the risk doesn't disappear once you're in your 20s," Prof. Large said. "What we're seeing suggests a cumulative effect, where harm builds up over time, a bit like alcohol or nicotine.".

Interestingly, the analysis did not identify a statistically significant difference in the timing of psychosis between teenage cannabis consumers and teenagers who did not use cannabis.

Industry observers note that however, the researchers cautioned that this finding does not necessarily mean younger cannabis users face no risk. Psychosis rarely develops before the middle teenage years, leaving relatively little opportunity for its onset to shift to an even younger age.

Recent findings suggest that "There may be a biological floor, in that there is only so much earlier that onset can be shifted. In younger groups, strong development, genetic or other psychosis risk factors may dominate, making any cannabis-related age shift harder to detect," Prof. Large remarked.

The researchers also stressed an crucial limitation. Because the analysis examined existing observational studies, it cannot establish that cannabis directly causes psychosis or makes the condition begin sooner. Demonstrating such a relationship experimentally would require research that deliberately exposed people to potential psychiatric harm, which would be unethical.

Nevertheless, Prof. Large believes the overall pattern provides meaningful evidence supporting a possible causal connection.

"But the consistency of the evidence, particularly the strong effect in older adults who likely have been using cannabis for longer, does support the theory that cannabis plays a causal role in the timing of psychosis onset, and possibly the onset of some cases among people who would not have otherwise developed psychosis.".

Upcoming Findings Challenge Assumptions About Cannabis After Age 25.

The latest research builds on two earlier investigations into cannabis use and the development of psychosis.

In a smaller 2011 meta-analysis led by Prof. Large, researchers found that psychosis began approximately 2.7 years earlier among cannabis customers. A separate 2015 analysis reported that psychosis typically developed 6.3 years after cannabis use began.

However, neither earlier investigation had enough information to determine how the relationship differed across age groups.

By incorporating a much larger body of research, the latest analysis allowed scientists to examine how the association changes across different stages of adulthood.

Lead author Carly Stevens, from UNSW's School of Biomedical Sciences, stated the findings undermine the idea that avoiding cannabis during adolescence is sufficient to eliminate its potential psychiatric dangers.

Sources indicate that "What we've found challenges the assumption that you'll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s; that's just not the case," Ms. Stevens noted.

"There's been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is notable, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone.".

Why Even a Few Years of Delayed Psychosis Matter.

Although a difference of two or three years might initially seem relatively small, the researchers emphasized that the timing of psychosis can have profound consequences for a person's future.

Industry observers note that the late teenage years and early adulthood are often periods when people complete their education, begin careers, establish relationships, and develop greater independence. Experiencing a serious psychiatric disorder earlier in life can interrupt these important milestones.

Sources indicate that "People may miss out on study, job opportunities, travel, and relationships in those years, and treatment can come with physical side effects that can make life harder as well," Ms. Stevens said.

Prof. Large emphasized the potential benefits of reducing or discontinuing cannabis use and the importance of delaying the onset of psychosis wherever possible.

According to recent reports, "It's a major illness, which robs you of your shared reality with family, friends and all those around you," he stated. "If we can delay psychosis by even a few years, people will be more likely to reach crucial milestones in education and training, and develop strong support networks, which can protect against psychosocial decline.".

In a recent development, the potential benefits could also extend to healthcare systems. According to Prof. Large, psychotic disorders account for as much as 3% of health-related spending in developed countries. Preventing or delaying the onset of these conditions could therefore have substantial social and economic benefits.

Scientists Call for Stronger Cannabis Health Warnings.

Despite the inability to establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship, the researchers believe their findings provide sufficient justification for stronger warnings about the possible psychiatric consequences of cannabis use.

Industry observers note that "We can't run direct experiments, so we have to go with the best evidence available," Prof. Large noted. "In my view, the threshold for health warnings about cannabis and psychosis has definitely been met.".

One concern is the growing popularity of medical cannabis. Prof. Large mentioned its increasing use as a therapeutic product may encourage some people to assume that it carries little risk.

He has also observed an increasing number of patients receiving treatment for psychosis who had previously been prescribed cannabis for medical conditions where evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited.

"It's got this therapeutic halo around it, which blinds people to the risk.".

It has been revealed that another emerging concern involves cannabis edibles, which can contain elevated concentrations of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main compound responsible for the drug's mind altering effects. The availability of products containing higher THC concentrations raises additional questions about possible psychiatric risks.

At the same time, Prof. Large acknowledged that cannabis legalization could create opportunities to reduce harm, even though it would also make cannabis easier to obtain.

Legal regulation could allow governments to establish limits on product potency, improve consumer education, introduce taxation, and require buyers to receive clear information about potential health consequences.

According to recent reports, "You could tax it, regulate it, and require people to show they understand the risks before buying," Prof. Large remarked.

More Research Needed on Long-Term Cannabis Exposure.

The researchers say further studies are necessary to understand the biological processes that might explain why the association between cannabis use and earlier psychosis becomes more pronounced with age.

In particular, they want to investigate whether repeated or prolonged cannabis exposure produces cumulative changes that influence when psychotic symptoms emerge.

They also recommend additional research focusing on older cannabis users, an increasingly vital population as medical cannabis becomes more common and products containing high concentrations of THC become more widely available.

Another priority is improving how cannabis exposure is measured. The researchers argue that future studies need clearer and more consistent methods for recording cannabis consumption so that findings can be compared more reliably.

Ultimately, the latest analysis highlights an important gap in public understanding of cannabis and mental health. While warnings have traditionally concentrated on teenage use, the findings suggest that potential psychiatric risks deserve attention throughout adulthood, particularly among people who continue using cannabis over many years.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This goes beyond your usual video game merchandise featuring the main characters.
  • Panini America announced its partnership with Rockstar Games on November 24.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been less than a week since Grand Theft Auto 6 came out, and Rockstar Games has already found another way to get us to spend money on the game. If you've been collecting sports cards while exploring Leonida, you'll soon be able to do the same outside the game. Rockstar has partnered with Panini America to bring these fictional sports trading cards to life, and they'll be out in December 2026.

This goes beyond your usual video game merchandise featuring the main characters. The cards are based on collectibles that actually exist within GTA 6's world, so you might recognize some of the athletes and teams when you open a pack. And if you're hoping to get your hands on some of the rarer cards, there are even a few that are limited to a single copy each.

Panini America announced its partnership with Rockstar Games on November 24. The officially licensed set is called the GTA VI: Sports Trading Card Collection, and it'll be the first trading card collaboration between the two companies.

If you've ever collected football or basketball cards, chances are you're already familiar with Panini. They're also known for reprinting comics in Europe, and I still have a copy of the X-Men: The Last Stand Annual 2007 published by Panini Books.

What's different this time is that instead of collecting cards featuring actual sports stars, you'll be collecting ones based on athletes from Rockstar's fictional universe. The promotional artwork demonstrates a mixture of illustrated cards and ones featuring character renders, much like those found in the game itself.

In a recent development, the cards will come in boxes containing four packs each. Panini claims a box will typically include two Rookie cards, a Retro card, an Illustrated card and four Special Silvers. These are average figures rather than guaranteed contents for every box.

Industry observers note that there'll also be different colored variants of the cards, including silver, pink, teal and light blue, along with team-colored parallels. The rarest variants have much smaller print runs. The Legend Bronze cards are numbered out of 49, the numbered Silver variants out of 25, and the Gold variants are one-of-a-kind cards.

Considering how many people are playing GTA 6 right now, I wouldn’t be surprised if some of the rare cards ended up selling for ridiculous prices.

Getting your hands on every variant, however, could be quite a challenge. Considering how many people are playing GTA 6 right now, I wouldn't be surprised if some of the rarer cards ended up selling for ridiculous prices.

Even if you don't care about the numbered cards, there's some appeal in having the regular ones. GTA's fictional athletes aren't exactly household names like the ones you'd find in Panini's other sports collections, but you can actually go looking for their cards in Leonida while playing the game.

According to recent reports, rockstar has been selling GTA merchandise for years, but this particular collaboration reminds me of the sort of extras that used to come with physical copies of video games. The maps that came with older GTA titles, for instance, were something you could actually use while playing and keep long after you were done with the game.

Ironically, GTA 6's boxed edition doesn't even come with a game disc. So it's nice to see Rockstar making something physical that draws directly from the game rather than simply putting its logo on another piece of merchandise.

Rockstar could've easily gone with a conventional trading card set featuring Jason, Lucia, and other major characters. Instead, it's making replicas of things you might stumble across while taking a break from the story. I'd love to see Rockstar do something similar with other fictional brands from the series, like Sprunk or eCola.

Unfortunately, Panini hasn't announced an exact release date, pricing, or which countries the cards will be available in.

Depending on when the cards go on sale in December, they could make for a pretty good Christmas gift for a GTA fan.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since 2023, the Recording Academy has included an official category for video game soundtracks, adding an air of legitimacy to a diverse musical medium we know and love.
  • It has been revealed that as is often the case, what stands out most about these nominees is how, generally speaking, they don't fully align with gaming culture's favorite soundtracks of the year, and instead often trend toward the most recognizable IP (often franchises with films) of the year.
  • Sources indicate that the standout here is Ghost of Yōtei, which is not an adaptation of the massive franchises the other games fall into.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 2023, the Recording Academy has included an official category for video game soundtracks, adding an air of legitimacy to a diverse musical medium we know and love. Today, we learned the list of nominees for the 2027 Grammy ceremony, and it's an interesting lineup. The nominations are as follows:.

It has been revealed that as is often the case, what stands out most about these nominees is how, generally speaking, they don't fully align with gaming culture's favorite soundtracks of the year, and instead often trend toward the most recognizable IP (often franchises with films) of the year. On that note, it's most surprising to see that Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora has been nominated for the third year in a row: once for the base game, once for the Secrets of the Spires DLC, and now for the From The Ashes DLC. None of these soundtracks are bad by any means, but their Grammy representation far outweighs their cultural footprint.

Sources indicate that the standout here is Ghost of Yōtei, which is not an adaptation of the massive franchises the other games fall into. However, it's also a Sony-published game, which have a pretty good track record of getting nominations, potentially due to the tech giant's massive presence in the music and film industries. Still, Ghost of Yōtei has a great, unique score that's deserving of its spot, and also one previously nominated for best music at the 2025 Game Awards. The Grammys accept any releases between October 1 of one year and September 30 of the following year, so Ghost of Yōtei barely made the cut for this window. The Game Awards nominees will be announced tomorrow – it will be interesting to see how much overlap there is between the categories.

It has been revealed that this batch of Grammy noms also has fewer recurring nominees than past years. This is Gordy Haab's third nomination (he won in 2024 for Star Wars Jedi: Survivor) and John Paesano's second nomination (he was nominated in 2025 for Marvel's Spider-Man 2). It's also the first year since the awards' creation without Bear McCreary or Austin Wintory nominations.

According to recent reports, last year's nominations left a sour taste in the mouths of many, with several DLC nominees and a complete lack of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, the year's standout hit that many specifically praised for its music. This year certainly has snubs (Mewgenics, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, and Control Resonant all come to mind), but none as egregious as last year.

What do you think was the best video game score from the last year? Let us know in the comments!

According to recent reports, diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

According to recent reports, the Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

Sources indicate that the livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the latest class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

What we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s latest region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two upcoming endgame modes in War Intends, and Echoing Hatred.

Recent findings suggest that war Prepares lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a new activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

We also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

Industry observers note that the Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

According to recent reports, reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as fresh quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

"Nobody was hurt" in a shooting last week near the California office of Clockwork Revolution developers InXile, both the studio and local police have confirmed. The incident, which took place on November 11th, is currently being investigated and police have reportedly taken a suspect into custody.

"Officers got there [on November 11th]," Tustin police sergeant Christopher Peterson said in statement to Aftermath. "They responded to a report of a drive-by shooting there. Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt. Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why.".

Industry observers note that "We’re relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," a spokesperson for InXile mentioned in a separate statement. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate.".

Recent findings suggest that inXile are set to release steampunk RPG Clockwork Revolution next year. The studio, developers of the likes of Wasteland 3 and The Bard's Tale IV, are one of the few Xbox-owned studios not to have been affected - at least as of writing - by Microsoft's ongoing mass layoffs this year.

Sources indicate that since being confirmed in 2023, Clockwork Revolution's dripped with Bioshock-ish vibes and popped up semi-regularly at Xbox showcases. "Wield the power of an incredible device to travel back in time, changing the past and rewriting the future of the city you call home: the vibrant steampunk metropolis of Avalon," reads its Steam synopsis. "In this immersive RPG, you'll step into the shoes of Morgan Vanette, a fully customizable player-character and member of the Rotten Row Hooligans. Travel between past and present as you battle the ruthless Lady Ironwood, who has been manipulating time to keep the working class struggling while amassing immense wealth and power.".

Best wishes to the staff at InXile, here's hoping that going forwards they're able to get with making what's looking to be an intriguingly funky game without enduring any more concerning incidents like this one.

This could be either latest updates for the game, unrelated to the DLC, or even new titles from one of the world’s most secluded dev teams.

Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO a little under two weeks ago after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (no relation), who formerly controlled Singaporean tech firm Megaspeed International and has been the subject of US national security concerns related to AI chip exports to China.

Following the admission, as well as reports of two other affairs with Nvidia employees, Huang resigned as Nvidia president, CEO, and board member. Last week, amid calls for Huang's return from tech CEOs and investors, the Nvidia board noted firmly that it would not reinstate him.

It has been revealed that cue the It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia title card: The gang reinstated him. On Monday, the Nvidia board remarked that it had "voted unanimously" to bring Huang back after receiving "input from senior levels of the United States government." Nvidia shares shot up 31.48% during Monday's trading.

Sources indicate that trump has taken credit for the change of heart. "I made the deal," he told CNBC. The President also posted a congratulatory AI-generated image depicting Huang as himself surviving an attempted assassination while holding up a red bra victoriously.

The news of Huang's reinstatement prompted a flurry of responses from US congressmembers on Monday.

"President Trump's direct involvement with Nvidia’s decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang raises serious national security and corruption questions. We must investigate these actions," mentioned California Democratic congressman Robert Garcia in a statement. "No president who has invested in a private tech giant should be involved in their board decisions. Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately.".

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It hasn't just been Democrats criticizing Huang's reinstatement.

Sources indicate that "Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking 'candor,'" stated Republican senator Pete Ricketts of Nebraska. "I've served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.".

"The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang," noted North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer. "The worst part of this is what we may never know. Congress should immediately pass the strictest export controls possible. I hope it’s not too late.".

Huang is set to testify before the US Senate next Thursday, December 3.

#132362. Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1814 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer.
  • In a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody.
  • Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer showed an elevated risk of developing tumors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common antibody found throughout the digestive tract may provide an unexpected defense against colon cancer. Researchers at Rockefeller University have discovered that these immune molecules help regulate the growth of cells lining the intestine, potentially preventing the uncontrolled cell division that can lead to tumors.

In a study published in Nature, scientists found that mice missing a type of antibody known as immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels of the antibody. The researchers also uncovered how this protection works. IgA attaches to cells along the intestinal lining and helps prevent them from multiplying too rapidly.

Even more promising, when the team administered IgA orally to mice that lacked the antibody, the animals no longer showed an elevated risk of developing tumors.

"One intriguing aspect of this work is that it highlights how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer," notes senior author Daniel Mucida, who leads Rockefeller's Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. "Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?".

The findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, a condition in which the body produces little or none of this antibody, face a greater risk of colorectal cancer. They also offer latest insight into how gut bacteria, immune defenses, and intestinal cells work together to influence cancer development, potentially even in people with otherwise healthy immune systems.

Why the Gut Contains So Much of This Antibody.

IgA is one of the immune system's most abundant antibodies in the digestive tract, where it provides an important early defense against potentially harmful microbes. Unlike antibodies that recognize a single specific target, IgA can interact with many different kinds of gut bacteria and even certain healthy cells belonging to the body.

Industry observers note that scientists have known for decades that the intestines contain unusually large quantities of IgA. However, the reasons for its abundance, and the full range of functions it performs, have remained incompletely understood.

Industry observers note that mucida's laboratory investigates how the intestine manages two essential but sometimes competing responsibilities. It must defend the body against dangerous microorganisms while allowing nutrients from food to pass into the bloodstream. Earlier research from his team has also helped explain how immune cells in the digestive tract contribute to food intolerances and allergies.

For the latest study, Gregory Donaldson, a former postdoctoral researcher at Rockefeller who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, set out to better understand how IgA interacts with intestinal bacteria and whether those interactions might influence the development of colon cancer.

It has been revealed that "We know these antibodies bind bacteria and, by doing so, can shape the microbiome," he says. "And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the U.S., is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease.".

The microbiome is the community of microorganisms living in and on the body. In the intestines, these microbes perform notable functions related to digestion and immune health, but certain bacteria can also contribute to disease under the wrong conditions.

Missing Gut Antibodies More Than Doubled Colon Tumors.

To investigate IgA's protective effects, Donaldson compared mice that could not produce the antibody with mice that had normal IgA levels. Both groups were raised together, allowing the researchers to control for differences in food and exposure to microorganisms.

The results revealed a striking difference. Animals without IgA developed substantially more colorectal tumors than their counterparts, consistent with the increased colorectal cancer risk observed in humans with IgA deficiency.

According to recent reports, the association was not limited to a single experimental setup. Researchers observed the same pattern using multiple models of colon cancer, strengthening the evidence that IgA plays a meaningful protective role.

"We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect," says Donaldson.

The team then tested whether replacing the missing antibody could reverse the effect. When mice lacking IgA received oral doses of the antibody, their increased susceptibility to colon tumors disappeared.

This result suggested that IgA does more than simply accompany other protective processes in the intestine. Its presence appears to directly influence conditions that determine whether tumors develop.

Scientists Discover a Natural Brake on Cancer Cell Growth.

Recent findings suggest that to understand the mechanism behind this protection, the researchers examined epithelial cells, which form the inner lining of the intestine. These cells are particularly vital because colon cancer begins when cells in this tissue undergo changes that allow them to grow uncontrollably.

The intestinal lining is constantly renewing itself. Older or damaged cells are replaced by upcoming ones, making controlled cell division essential for keeping the digestive tract healthy. However, when the signals that regulate this process become disrupted, excessive growth can create opportunities for cancer to develop.

In mice without IgA, the researchers identified changes in gene activity associated with cell proliferation, the process through which cells divide and increase in number. Crucially, these changes appeared before any tumors became visible, suggesting that the antibody helps regulate an early step in cancer development.

"We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this," Donaldson claims.

The researchers suspected that IgA was interacting with a specific molecular structure on the surface of intestinal cells, allowing it to influence how those cells behaved.

Gabriella Lima dos Reis, the study's second author and a graduate student working in Gabriel Victora's laboratory, investigated a promising candidate called DMBT1.

Industry observers note that DMBT1 is a receptor found on the surface of epithelial cells that can bind to IgA. Previous research had connected it to several types of cancer, but scientists had not established precisely how it functions in the development of colon tumors.

How Gut Bacteria and IgA Control Tumor Formation.

Further experiments revealed that DMBT1 plays two very different roles depending on whether IgA is present.

In a recent development, when intestinal bacteria are present, DMBT1 activates signals that encourage epithelial cells to divide. This response is part of the normal activity of the intestinal lining, which must continually replace cells to maintain its protective barrier.

Recent findings suggest that igA helps keep that growth under control. When the antibody binds to DMBT1, it restrains the receptor's activity, effectively acting as a brake on cell proliferation.

Recent findings suggest that without IgA, however, DMBT1 signaling can continue without sufficient restraint. Intestinal cells then divide more rapidly than they should, increasing the likelihood that tumors will develop.

The researchers confirmed that this excessive growth depends on several interacting factors. When gut bacteria were absent, DMBT1 signaling was disabled, or normal amounts of IgA were available, epithelial cell division remained under control.

Together, these findings reveal how a common immune molecule helps maintain the delicate balance between necessary tissue renewal and potentially dangerous overgrowth.

Sources indicate that "If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function -- responding to bacteria by producing new cells -- can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer," Mucida indicates. "We think this homeostatic effect is IgA's main function. This was a substantial surprise.".

Sources indicate that homeostasis refers to the body's ability to maintain stable, healthy conditions despite constant changes in its environment. In this case, IgA appears to support that balance by preventing normal intestinal cell renewal from becoming excessive.

A New Possibility for Preventing Colon Cancer.

By identifying DMBT1's normal role in intestinal cells, the Rockefeller team has uncovered a potential target for future colon cancer prevention strategies.

Instead of waiting until a tumor develops and then attempting to destroy it, researchers may eventually be able to influence the biological signals that make tumors more likely to form.

"Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor," Mucida states. "We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point.".

According to recent reports, colon polyps are growths that develop along the inner lining of the large intestine. Although many are harmless, some can eventually become cancerous. Removing them during a colonoscopy can reduce cancer risk, but researchers are interested in finding additional ways to prevent future tumors from developing.

The newly identified IgA and DMBT1 pathway could offer one such opportunity, although additional research is needed to determine whether targeting it would be effective and safe in humans.

Could Beneficial Gut Bacteria Help Prevent Cancer?

It has been revealed that the discovery also raises another intriguing possibility. Certain intestinal bacteria may actively help protect against cancer by influencing how epithelial cells behave or by encouraging the production of protective antibodies.

While much of the research into the gut microbiome and cancer has focused on harmful bacteria that promote tumor formation or accelerate cancer growth, some microbes may have the opposite effect.

"What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well," Donaldson notes. "A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it's one direction that we could look towards in the future.".

Such an approach would aim to use beneficial microorganisms to stimulate the body's existing protective mechanisms rather than directly attacking cancer cells. However, the idea remains speculative, and the mouse experiments do not establish that taking IgA supplements or probiotics can prevent colon cancer in people.

For now, the findings provide a clearer picture of how the immune system and gut microbiome cooperate to maintain healthy intestinal tissue. They also suggest that some of the body's most important defenses against cancer may operate long before the disease becomes detectable.

Mucida adds, "Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health.".

Industry observers note that keiko’s NRG spell ran from 12 November 2025 to 21 October 2026. He finished third at Masters Santiago 2026. He also placed third in both VCT Americas Stage 1 and Stage 2. At Champions 2026 he finished joint fifth to sixth.

Sentinels reached no international event in 2026. The team went out of that year’s Kickoff in the bottom four. It then missed the playoffs in both Stage 1 and Stage 2. Adding a player with that run of results is consistent with a side trying to close the gap swiftly.

His move to Sentinels places a British player at the centre of a rebuilt Americas contender.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BioWare made one of the most beloved RPGs of all time with Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, but it was Obisidan that followed up with Knights of the Old Republic 2: The Sith Lords, another massively popular game. It's somewhat well-documented that publisher LucasArts wanted the sequel done promptly and that BioWare turned down the project for that reason, but in a upcoming interview, BioWare veteran John Winski confirms that's the case and even puts an exact number on LucasArts' request.

Talking to Pembridge TV, Winski notes LucasArts approached BioWare to develop Knights of the Old Republic 2 and asked for the project to be completed in just 18 months. "When LucasArts came to us and remarked, 'hey, you want to make a sequel?' We were like, 'OK,' and they gave us 18 months, and we were like, 'nope. No. We can't do it in 18 months. That's not enough time'," says Winski. "And then Obsidian was like, 'we'll try.'".

Sources indicate that try, Obsidian did, and for the most part, it succeeded. Winski rightfully points out Knights of the Old Republic 2 was released in a pretty sorry state, or in his words, not "totally finished," but he acknowledges that "a lot of people really love it" despite an "unreasonable" development cycle set by LucasArts. "It's still something that is worth having been done," he adds.

It has been revealed that it really is remarkable how successful Obsidian was in following up such a celebrated release, and the very first RPG adaptation of Star Wars, with a game almost equally as beloved, all under pressure from the rights holder to deliver in an incredibly short timeframe. Just a couple of years later, the studio managed a similar feat with the release of Neverwinter Nights 2, yet another acclaimed RPG sequel to a BioWare-developed title. Leave it to Obsidian, I suppose.

Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic director isn't worried about pressure from RPG fans since his team already made KOTOR and Mass Effect: "We're not trying to fill someone else's shoes".

Take-Two's GTA 6 PC Port Crackdown Has Already Taken Down Over 3,000 Repositories

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that leonida was named after the fictional state in which GTA 6 takes place, and it was one of several attempts to get the console version running on a computer.
  • The developers had asked consumers to supply their own game files, but Take-Two argues that the project was designed specifically to make use of the leaked build.
  • It has been revealed that gitHub says it acted on the entire network of 3,007 repositories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that leonida was named after the fictional state in which GTA 6 takes place, and it was one of several attempts to get the console version running on a computer. Unlike some of the fan-made PC ports we've seen for older console games, though, this one was being developed using a build of a game that had only just come out.

The developers had asked consumers to supply their own game files, but Take-Two argues that the project was designed specifically to make use of the leaked build. The manufacturer requested that GitHub take down Leonida and its forks, arguing that the alleged infringement couldn't be addressed without disabling the repositories altogether.

It has been revealed that gitHub says it acted on the entire network of 3,007 repositories. That number includes forks, which are essentially copies of a repository that other GitHub users can work on independently. That doesn't mean there were 3,007 different GTA 6 PC ports in development, though.

An Xbox Series build of GTA 6 was leaked on November 20, with the Leonida repository appearing a day later.

Recent findings suggest that according to PC Gamer, the team appeared to have reached the game's splash screen during a livestream before it crashed. The project's lead developer, NotRexed, subsequently announced their departure, citing the loss of the Discord server as well as the pressure of managing the community alongside school and sports.

According to recent reports, take-Two's takedown hasn't put an end to Leonida, either. According to the same report, others have already tried to pick up where the original developer left off.

It's a familiar situation for those of us who primarily play on PC. GTA 4 came to PC several months after its console debut, while we had to wait more than a year and a half after GTA 5's original launch for its PC version. Even Red Dead Redemption 2 took roughly a year to make its way over.

In a recent development, the difference this time is that a report has suggested GTA 6 could arrive on PC in the first quarter of 2027. If that turns out to be true, the wait would be much shorter than it was for Rockstar's last two major releases. There hasn't been an official announcement confirming that release window, however.

Recent findings suggest that getting GTA 6 to boot on a PC and getting it to run well enough to play through the entire game are two very different things. Just look at how badly Rockstar handled GTA 4's PC port. Even hardware that far exceeded the game's original system requirements struggled to run it smoothly, and Rockstar never bothered to properly fix it.

Industry observers note that modders have spent years ironing out its performance complications and bugs, and while that's still an ongoing process, I'd argue 2026 has been the best year yet to play GTA 4 on PC. Even if one of these unofficial efforts eventually makes it past the splash screen, there's no telling how well the game will run on a typical gaming PC or whether it'll have major bugs throughout the story.

According to recent reports, hopefully, Rockstar won't keep us in the dark for too long regarding the official PC version. Even an approximate release window would be welcome at this point, especially for anyone holding off on buying a console just to play GTA 6.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover a newly introduced type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression.
  • Industry observers note that circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A newly identified form of depression may help explain why some people struggle to find relief from commonly prescribed antidepressants. Researchers at the University of Sydney have discovered a subtype called "circadian depression," which appears to be closely connected to the body's internal biological clock.

Industry observers note that the discovery emerged from an analysis of clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression. Nearly one-quarter of the participants in the study, which focused on people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, demonstrated characteristics of this newly identified subtype.

Industry observers note that circadian depression is associated with the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps regulate when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy. People with this form of depression tend to respond less favorably to common serotonin-based antidepressants. However, treatments that target the brain circuits involved in controlling circadian rhythms, including melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants and light therapy, may offer more effective options.

Published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, the findings shed light on the genetic factors associated with this subtype and offer a possible explanation for why widely used medications such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) are less effective for some patients.

A Hidden Type of Depression Affecting Nearly One in Four Patients Studied.

Sources indicate that to investigate the biological differences between forms of depression, researchers examined information collected through the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Their analysis included clinical histories and genetic data from more than 10,000 people who had experienced depression.

In a recent development, the researchers identified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Several recognizable patterns distinguished these individuals from other people with depression.

Those with the circadian subtype were more likely to experience seasonal changes in their depression, sleep for longer periods when depressed, and wake up feeling exhausted despite spending more time in bed. They were also more likely to be night owls, meaning they naturally preferred staying awake late and waking later in the day.

It has been revealed that the differences extended beyond sleep patterns. Depression often began earlier in life for these individuals, and their symptoms tended to be more severe (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). Genetic analysis also revealed an increased predisposition to inflammatory and cardiovascular health problems, along with major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

According to recent reports, first author Dr. Emiliana Tonini from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Center stated:.

"Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

"Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them.".

Why Common Antidepressants May Be Less Effective.

One of the most notable implications of the discovery involves how depression is treated.

Medications such as SSRIs and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are generally among the first treatments offered to people diagnosed with depression. These drugs work by influencing chemical messengers in the brain that help regulate mood.

Sources indicate that however, the researchers found that these medications tend to be less effective for people with circadian depression. Individuals with this subtype also experience more side effects, suggesting that conventional antidepressants may not be the best initial approach for everyone.

Because circadian depression is closely associated with the body's internal clock, therapies designed to influence that clock may be particularly useful. Light therapy, for example, uses controlled exposure to bright light to help regulate biological rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone involved in signaling when the body should prepare for sleep, and antidepressants that target melatonin pathways may also be relevant treatment options.

Sources indicate that co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse from the Brain and Mind Center explained:.

"Because circadian depression is linked to people's internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.

"For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is vital to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.".

A New Approach Could Improve Depression Treatment in Young People.

Recognizing circadian depression earlier could be especially vital for younger patients, who may otherwise spend valuable time trying medications that are less suited to their particular form of depression.

Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist, warned that failing to identify this subtype in young people can contribute to unsuccessful early treatments and unnecessary side effects.

The findings highlight the importance of recognizing that depression is not a single, uniform condition. Different biological mechanisms may contribute to similar symptoms, meaning that treatments effective for one person may provide much less benefit to another.

By identifying patients whose depression is closely tied to circadian rhythms, clinicians may be able to offer more targeted treatments earlier rather than relying on the same initial medication approach for everyone.

"We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

"Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition.".

Materials provided by University of Sydney. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nioh 3 has received a hot latest enhancement that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest patch, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for enhancement 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an matter that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Sources indicate that team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s enhancement takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an glitch that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Sources indicate that hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

Sources indicate that 90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the company contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent manufacturer Take-Two quickly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely shows anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

Tech giant of Heroes 3: Operation Torch Review

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Firm of Heroes 3 has come a long way since its 2023 release, slowly making its way to the real-time strategy hall of fame after a rather rough start.
  • It has been revealed that patch 3.0 helped bring the game to its full potential, but mechanical polish only goes so far.
  • The dynamic campaign remains the highlight of Organization of Heroes 3, but thanks to Operation Torch, the game finally has a scripted, story campaign that’s worth the trouble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Firm of Heroes 3 has come a long way since its 2023 release, slowly making its way to the real-time strategy hall of fame after a rather rough start. And yet, until now, something was missing.

It has been revealed that patch 3.0 helped bring the game to its full potential, but mechanical polish only goes so far. Until recently, Company of Heroes 3 was a brilliant strategy game with strong mechanics that lend themselves well to single-player, but this was offset by a lack of quality content you could go through solo.

The dynamic campaign remains the highlight of Organization of Heroes 3, but thanks to Operation Torch, the game finally has a scripted, story campaign that’s worth the trouble.

Operation Torch is the first single-player campaign DLC for Tech giant of Heroes 3. It was preceded by the unorthodox yet highly entertaining Final Stand tower defence DLC, but surviving wave after wave of German tanks is no substitute for a touching story.

Sources indicate that in that sense, the choice to depict Operation Torch is a poetic one. While American forces were being put through wringer in Pacific islands, the US had yet to launch any major land operations against the Germans and Italians.

Recent findings suggest that the North Africa landings sent a green Army against veteran enemies. The Americans turned out to be quite adept at learning on the job, but the lessons there were written in blood. As a DLC, Operation Torch is similar.

Company of Heroes 3 emerges victorious once you see it through, but that success comes on the back of some blunders and failures that I hope are not repeated if or when Relic Entertainment decides another story-driven DLC is due.

The DLC focuses on three American soldiers from the US Army’s 34th Infantry Division, all the way from the landings in Algeria to the crushing of Axis resistance in Tunisia.

As far as individual story beats go, Operation Torch is adequate. Becker, Russo and Flanagan are likeable and quite distinct, and their commentary enhances the missions for the most part. There are some occasional immersion-breaking bits that strike out as silly, just about all of them relating to ‘tutorial’ speech.

For example, in a rather late mission in the campaign, Becker instructs us to defend fuel points because “we need the fuel to build tanks.” Well yes, Colonel, in game we do, but I’m operating under the assumption that these tanks were manufactured in a plant somewhere in Detroit rather than spontaneously spawned through good vibes and virtual resources somewhere in Tunisia.

This is nowhere near as egregious as in the much-maligned Rommel campaign that comes with the base game, but it would have been nice to have the option to disable tutorial-style objectives and commentary for people who are familiar with the game or who are going for a second playthrough.

I need to emphasize repeat playthroughs here because, although Operation Torch is a linear, story-based DLC, it incorporates lessons from other Manufacturer of Heroes 3 releases that make it more replayable than other campaigns in a similar vein.

Recent findings suggest that most missions are fairly open-ended in terms of how you can approach them. This is complemented by a decent degree of customization after each mission depending on how you accomplish both primary and secondary objectives. The Italy campaign had similar choices, but the Operation Torch system is closer to that of the Final Stand DLC.

The effects of the upgrades you pick are rather tangible. For example, early on, I managed to unlock M3 assault halftracks as a command call-in. Despite being rather underwhelming in their basic battle taxi configuration, these can be converted into game-changers.

The Americans turned out to be quite adept at learning on the job, but the lessons there were written in blood.

According to recent reports, many of my missions were saved because I was able to bring in an M3 converted into 75mm gun carriers that provided quick, on-call artillery support to break down defenses. When dug in myself, the M16 variant with the .50 quad-mounts made mince out of Axis infantry, allowing outnumbered defenders to hold out. All of this could have gone differently had I chosen another upgrade perk, which would have had its own advantages.

Final Stand’s influence is particularly felt in those defensive scenarios, where its wave mechanics reach their zenith.

Base game mechanics sometimes make these last stands slightly less dramatic than they could be at first, primarily because, as in real life, liberal application of engineering obstacles and overlapping fields of fire make incoming waves trivial. That false sense of safety comes apart spectacularly once heavier armor rolls in and you learn that Bazookas can’t dent it.

Relic managed to craft missions that reward sound tactics. Generally speaking, if it works in real life, it will work here. There is one exception that deserves its own section, and that’s the abysmal commando raid mission.

It has been revealed that when the Operation Torch announcement came about late last month, the commando gameplay was by far the most exciting part. I’ve been counting the days until SAS: Rogue Heroes comes back for its third season, and I was hoping the commando levels would be a good way to make the wait easier. I was sorely mistaken, I’m afraid.

In a recent development, the level where you plant explosive charges is an affront to modern game design, primarily because it is just… Pac-Man. With guns.

Sources indicate that you play one lonely commando, and your job is to slip by German patrols to plant demolition charges on 88mm guns. Every time you die (which, in my experience, is a lot), you respawn on the last checkpoint. Besides snipers, taking out any enemy does virtually nothing as they respawn almost immediately as well.

Sources indicate that the result is a level that’s both archaic and devoid of meaning. There’s no way to fail the mission, as you just keep sending more and more single commandos into the breech, the Germans reciprocate, and you’re sitting there playing Pac-Man timing patrol movement patterns for a dry 30 minutes.

The mission is a one off, much like the American debacle in the Kasserine Pass in February 1943, but it leaves a mark on what’s otherwise a well-built campaign with strong design and balancing.

Playing Operation Torch and the Italy campaign back-to-back has been great because you get to see how far Allied land operations in the Mediterranean Theater of Operations have come from the shaky landings in Algeria to the assault on Monte Cassino that opened the road to Rome.

It’s nice to see an oft-forgotten part of World War 2 history given the attention it deserves. The British and German versions of the fight for North Africa have been told a million times over, but with a few exceptions (most notably Call of Duty 2: Big Red One), the American African campaign is constantly overshadowed by later exploits in Europe and the Pacific.

Operation Torch also lays out a blueprint for potential future DLCs that focus on telling stories, rather than just adding new units to the same old multiplayer slog. The combined force of this DLC with update 3.0 released earlier this month puts Company of Heroes 3 in the spot it was always meant to occupy since its launch.

Industry observers note that relic made a bold choice in depicting Operation Torch to this degree, and it paid off in spades. Company of Heroes 3 mechanics come alive in a fight that doesn’t get the attention it deserves, in spite of occasional hiccups. The first narrative-driven DLC for the game shows that there’s plenty of untapped potential in it, and it’s left me hoping more of them will come.

Latest Update: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, researchers in Japan have developed a promising new treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed.
  • Sources indicate that developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light.
  • Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, researchers in Japan have developed a promising new treatment for gum disease that kills harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed. Unlike conventional approaches that can eliminate both good and bad bacteria, the new therapy is designed to target specific microbes responsible for damaging gums and the bone that supports teeth.

Sources indicate that developed by scientists at Nagoya University, the treatment combines antibodies obtained from egg yolks with near-infrared light. Early experiments in human cell cultures and mice suggest that it could offer a more precise way to combat periodontitis, a serious form of gum disease that can eventually lead to tooth loss. The findings were published in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

Why Conventional Gum Disease Treatments Can Cause Problems.

The human mouth contains a complex community of microorganisms, many of which play crucial roles in maintaining oral health. Problems can arise when harmful bacteria multiply and disturb this delicate balance.

It has been revealed that one particularly troublesome species is Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis), which scientists classify as a keystone pathogen. This means it can have an outsized influence on the surrounding microbial community, even when it is not especially abundant. By promoting inflammation and disrupting the normal balance of oral bacteria, it can contribute to the destruction of the bone that holds teeth in place.

Sources indicate that treating periodontitis often involves eliminating the bacteria responsible for the infection. However, some existing antimicrobial treatments do not distinguish between harmful organisms and microbes that help maintain a healthy mouth.

In a recent development, "Current treatments for periodontitis, including antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT), eliminate both pathogenic and beneficial oral bacteria," mentioned Kazuhide Sato, one of the corresponding authors and a lecturer at Nagoya University. "These approaches often disrupt the entire oral microbial ecosystem and can also release lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an endotoxin that may exacerbate inflammation.".

Scientists Adapt Cancer Therapy to Target Gum Disease Bacteria.

To overcome these limitations, the Nagoya University team turned to a technology originally designed to treat cancer. Known as near-infrared photoimmunotherapy, it uses antibodies linked to a light-sensitive dye to recognize specific targets. Once the compound attaches to its intended target, exposure to near-infrared light activates the dye and produces a damaging effect.

Sources indicate that the researchers adapted this strategy to attack P. gingivalis without unnecessarily disturbing other oral bacteria. Their approach relies on IgY, a type of antibody collected from the egg yolks of hens that have been immunized against the pathogen.

Egg yolk antibodies offer a practical advantage because they can be produced in large quantities at relatively low cost. This could make them an attractive option for developing targeted treatments that are affordable and scalable.

Industry observers note that the resulting technology, called near-infrared photo-antibacterial targeting therapy (NIR-PAT²), was developed by researchers at Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine. The team included first author Hiroshi Maruyama, Professor Hideharu Hibi, and corresponding authors Sato and Kiyoshi Sakai.

Industry observers note that to determine whether the treatment could destroy harmful bacteria while protecting healthy tissue, the researchers tested it in human cell cultures and mice. They also compared its effects with those of conventional antimicrobial therapies.

Light-Activated Antibodies Destroy Harmful Bacteria.

In a recent development, laboratory experiments highlighted that the antibody and dye combination attached specifically to P. gingivalis. Other bacterial species and healthy human gum cells were left unaffected.

When the researchers illuminated the targeted bacteria with near-infrared light, the activated dye damaged their outer membranes, ultimately killing them.

According to recent reports, microscopic examination revealed an vital difference between this technique and conventional antimicrobial light therapy. Bacteria exposed to the upcoming treatment developed tiny openings in their membranes but largely maintained their overall shape. By contrast, conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy caused the bacteria to break apart completely.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction matters because destroying bacterial cells can release substances that contribute to inflammation. Preserving the overall structure of the targeted bacteria, even after killing them, could help limit this unwanted effect.

The researchers also examined how the treatments affected healthy human gum cells. Their targeted therapy caused no detectable harm to these cells, while conventional antimicrobial photodynamic therapy produced cellular damage and slowed healing.

Newly introduced Treatment Reduces Bone Loss in Mice.

The team next investigated whether these laboratory findings would translate into meaningful improvements in gum disease.

In mice with periodontitis, the experimental therapy significantly reduced the loss of alveolar bone, the part of the jawbone that surrounds and supports teeth. Preventing this type of bone deterioration is especially important because advanced periodontitis can loosen teeth and eventually cause them to fall out.

In a recent development, analysis of the animals' saliva revealed another encouraging result. The treatment reduced P. gingivalis while preserving beneficial Streptococcus bacteria, helping maintain a healthier balance of microorganisms in the mouth.

Conventional antibiotics and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy, on the other hand, eliminated both harmful and beneficial bacteria in the experiments, causing broader disruption to the oral microbial community.

"Results demonstrated that, unlike antibiotics or standard light therapy, this approach selectively removes the primary pathogenic species while preserving the remainder of the oral bacterial community," Sato said.

Together, the findings suggest that targeting individual disease-causing bacteria could help control gum disease while avoiding some of the unintended consequences of broader antimicrobial treatments.

AI Could Help Develop More Precise Gum Disease Treatments.

Although the early results are promising, the researchers recognize that periodontitis is a complex disease involving multiple bacterial species. Eliminating P. gingivalis alone may not be sufficient to treat every case.

To address this challenge, the team plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) to examine publicly available information about oral bacteria. By identifying other vital microorganisms and studying how different species interact, they hope to uncover additional targets for future therapies.

Sources indicate that the researchers also see potential implications beyond oral health. Periodontitis has been linked to several other medical conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that understanding the relationships between oral bacteria and these conditions could eventually help scientists identify which patients are most likely to benefit from specific treatments. AI analysis may play a role in making those decisions and guiding the development of more personalized approaches to gum disease.

For now, the therapy remains experimental, with its effectiveness demonstrated in laboratory studies and mice rather than human clinical trials. However, the findings point toward a possible future in which treating gum disease means selectively removing harmful bacteria instead of disrupting the entire microbial community that helps keep the mouth healthy.
